Phillips c. Douek

2020 QCCS 1048

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

_____________________

[
1
]

This case primarily concerns the validity of
three notarial wills made by the late Albert Douek during the six months
preceding his death on October 21, 2012, at the age of 91. In the first will,
made in April 2012, Mr. Douek bequeathed to the plaintiff — his longstanding
de
facto
spouse — the sum of $700,000. However, Ms. Phillips was not mentioned
in the other two wills Mr. Douek made in September 2012 and in which he left one
half of his property to his wife and the other half to his two daughters.

[
2
]

Ms. Phillips challenges the validity of the
September 2012 wills on the ground that they result from the undue influence of
Mr. Douek’s daughters — the defendants Ms. Nicole Madger Douek and
Ms. Maureen Rosen Douek —, who allegedly deceived their father into
believing that she was having an affair with a tennis pro. Seeking to benefit
from the April 2012 will, Ms. Phillips is claiming from Mr. Douek’s succession
the sum of $700,000.
[1]

She is also claiming the sum of $275,000, which Mr. Douek allegedly gave her,
shortly before his death, by way of a cheque which his bank refused to honour
for reasons that later turned out to be unjustified.

[
3
]

In the originating application she filed in
August 2013, Ms. Phillips also challenged the September 2012 wills on grounds
of incapacity. Pursuant to a bifurcation order made by Chief Justice Jacques R.
Fournier in May 2017, a first trial addressing that issue was held in
March 2018. In August 2018, the Court found that the September 2012 wills and
the other legal documents signed by Mr. Douek during that period were not
invalid on grounds of incapacity.
[2]

[
4
]

The defendants argue that Ms. Phillips’ undue
influence argument is ill-founded and that the September 2012 wills are valid.
As a result, they further contend, the April 2012 will is no longer valid and
Ms. Phillips has no claim thereunder. They further argue that Ms. Phillips’
claim under the April 2012 will ought to fail even if the September 2012 wills
were found to be invalid, firstly because that April 2012 will was made as a
result of undue influence, but also on grounds of unworthiness (article 621
C.C.Q.
).
Moreover, the defendants dispute Ms. Phillips’ $275,000 claim on the ground
that, although the cheque in question bears Mr. Douek’s signature, she
wrote it to herself without his authorization. They add that Ms. Phillips
engaged in similarly fraudulent transactions throughout 2012 and that she must
reimburse the value thereof to Mr. Douek’s succession. The defendants also
contend, in the alternative, that the alleged $275,000 gift is null as having
been made
mortis causa
. Lastly, the defendants contend that a
transaction that took place in April 2012 and pursuant to which Mr. Douek
transferred to Ms. Phillips his undivided interest in their residential
property ought to be revoked on grounds of coercion and ingratitude (article
1836, 2
nd
para.
C.C.Q.
).

I.
Context

[
5
]

Albert Douek, who was born in Egypt in 1921, married
the defendant Ms. Bertha Goliger Douek in 1949. They immigrated to Canada in
the late 1950s with their two daughters. Upon his arrival in Canada, Mr. Douek
started a business which was successful to such an extent that, during the
following decades, he became very wealthy.

[
6
]

Ms. Phillips and Mr. Douek met in 1982 and they
became romantically involved a few years later. Mr. Douek and Ms. Goliger Douek
never divorced. Separation from bed and board proceedings were commenced by Ms.
Goliger Douek in 1990, but they were eventually abandoned.
[3]
In the early 2000s, Ms. Phillips and Mr.
Douek started cohabiting in a newly built luxury house that they co-owned in
equal shares and that is located in Montreal’s Côte-Saint-Luc neighbourhood.
[4]
Mr. Douek lived in that house with Ms. Phillips until shortly
before his death in October 2012.

[
7
]

Over the years, Mr. Douek provided for Ms.
Phillips in various ways. The acquisition and building of the Côte-Saint-Luc house
was for the most part — if not entirely
[5]
—
paid for by Mr. Douek. Furthermore, while they were living together,
Ms. Phillips, who did not work, received from Mr. Douek a monthly
allowance of $3,000.
[6]
She also received substantial financial gifts. For example, in 2011
and 2012, in addition to her monthly allowance, she received payments totalling
more than $400,000.
[7]
Moreover, in the spring of 2012, Mr. Douek
bought her a car worth nearly $100,000.
[8]
There is a dispute between the parties as to whether
Ms. Phillips misappropriated some of the sums she received from Mr. Douek.

[
8
]

The wills at issue in this case are not the only ones that Mr. Douek
made during his lifetime. In his first will, made before a notary in 1974, he
instituted Ms. Goliger Douek as his sole universal legatee.
[9]
In 2000, he signed a notarial codicil that modified his 1974 will
and bequeathed to Ms. Phillips his share of the Côte-Saint-Luc property while
leaving the remainder of his property to Ms. Goliger Douek.
[10]
Twelve years later, in the winter of 2012, Mr. Douek — through
a handwritten codicil — modified his 2000 will so as to leave the remainder of
his property to his two daughters instead of Ms. Goliger Douek.
[11]

[
9
]

It is also in the winter of 2012 that Mr. Douek,
who was already suffering from macular degeneration — among other ailments —,
was diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia.
[12]

[
10
]

In April of that year, shortly before the start
of chemotherapy, Mr. Douek signed two notarial acts before notary Jamie Malus.
Pursuant to one of these acts, he transferred his share of the Côte-Saint-Luc
property to Ms. Phillips for the sum of one dollar.
[13]
The
second notarial act is a will by which Mr. Douek revoked his previous
wills and testamentary dispositions, bequeathed the sum of $700,000 to Ms.
Phillips, and expressed the intention to leave to Ms. Goliger Douek two
properties — one located in the Town of Mount Royal, the other in Florida —
while leaving the remainder of his property to Ms. Goliger Douek and his two
daughters, in equal shares.
[14]
In addition, Mr. Douek made individual gifts of $25,000 to
several persons, including his grandchildren and Ms. Phillips’ son. The will
also contained two clauses addressing what was to occur in the event that
either the gifts made to Ms. Phillips or the transfer of his share of the
Côte-Saint-Luc property were challenged by an interested party. These clauses,
which reflect Mr. Douek’s awareness of the tense relationship between his
daughters and Ms. Phillips, read as follows:
[15]

(d)        in the event that any proceeding is taken
by an interested party with respect to a bequest made to my dear friend ROSLYN
GOTHELF [Ms. Phillips] pursuant to the provisions of my Last Will and Testament
and/or pertaining to any gift made by me during my lifetime to my dear friend
ROSLYN GOTHELF, I hereby direct my Trustees to transfer and deliver the sum of
THREE HUNDRED AND SEVENTY-FIVE THOUSAND DOLLARS ($375,000) in outright and
absolute ownership to my dear friend ROSLYN GOTHELF, such bequest shall be made
irrespective of the outcome of the said proceeding;

(e)        in the event that the transfer made by me
during my lifetime of my interest in the immovable property located at [...],
Cote Saint-Luc, Quebec, [...] with ail the furniture, equipment and other
contents and accessories in or about the said property (collectively the “CSL
Property") to my dear friend ROSLYN GOTHELF is successfully challenged, I
direct my Trustees to transfer and deliver to my dear friend ROSLYN GOTHELF in
outright and absolute ownership my interest in the said CSL Property, which
includes all the furniture, equipment and other contents and accessories in or
about the said property;

[
11
]

In August 2012, Mr. Douek developed the
impression that his health was deteriorating, notably because he was feeling
increasingly tired. On August 28, he was admitted to Montreal’s Jewish General
Hospital.
[16]

[
12
]

Early in the morning of August 30, Mr. Douek was
found lying in a pool of blood in his hospital room. The medical record shows
that he had sustained head injuries and that he was suffering from respiratory
complications as a result of a fall.
[17]
Mr.
Douek was immediately transferred to the hospital’s intensive care unit (“ICU”),
where he stayed — intubated, medicated and sedated — for five days.
[18]

[
13
]

Meanwhile, on August 31, Ms. Phillips deposited
a cheque in the amount of $275,000 in one of her bank accounts. The cheque was
dated August 26 and it was purportedly made by Mr. Douek.
[19]
It is the defendants’ contention that, although the cheque bears
Mr. Douek’s signature, Ms. Phillips wrote it to herself without his
authorization.

[
14
]

Ms. Phillips argues that, while he was in the
ICU, Mr. Douek was pressured by his daughters to change his will. To that end,
she relies — among other things — on the testimony of Ms. Angela Santullo,
whose mother was also in the ICU in early September 2012. During the trial, Ms.
Santullo stated that, while in the vicinity of the ICU, she had overheard a
conversation during which Ms. Rosen Douek had mentioned that the family needed
to convince Mr. Douek to change his will, and that he should be told that
Ms. Phillips had been romantically involved with someone else.

[
15
]

On Sunday, September 2, 2012, while he was still
in the ICU, Mr. Douek signed two legal documents. One is a two-page quit claim
deed that was provided by his daughter Maureen and that was aimed at
transferring his interest in the Florida property to Ms. Goliger Douek.
[20]
The other document is a three-page notarial will.
[21]
It was prepared that afternoon by notary Dan Armand Derhy, who had
been informed by the family, earlier that day, of Mr. Douek’s desire to
make a new will.
[22]
The will indicates that Mr. Douek wished, firstly, to revoke his previous
wills and testamentary dispositions and, secondly, to leave one half of his
property to Ms. Goliger Douek and the other half to his two daughters. Ms.
Phillips is not mentioned in that will.

[
16
]

During that meeting with Mtre Derhy, Mr. Douek
was intubated and could only express himself in writing. In addition to
conveying his instructions about the will he wished to make, he wrote the
following while he was alone with Mtre Derhy:
[23]

Ce que j’ai donné elle Roslyn
PHILLIPS peut le garder

Roselyn PHILIPPS je coné tout ce qui
passez avec le pro tennis

[Reproduced as in the
original]

[
17
]

On September 4, 2012, the amount of the cheque
that Ms. Phillips had deposited on August 31 was debited from Mr. Douek’s
account.
[24]
Shortly thereafter, during the course of a verification triggered
by the transaction’s amount, an issue arose as to whether the signature on the
cheque was indeed Mr. Douek’s. After a representative of the bank,
Ms. Carol Edwards, unsuccessfully tried to reach him on September 5, Ms. Phillips’
account was debited and Mr. Douek’s account was credited for the amount of the
cheque.
[25]
The following day, Ms. Edwards reached Mr.
Douek — who was then out of the ICU
[26]
—
by phone. She told him about the cheque for $275,000 made out to Ms. Phillips.
Mr. Douek replied that he did not recall making that cheque and he instructed
the bank’s representative to block his account.
[27]

Later that day, he provided the bank with written confirmation that no cheque
was to go through his account until further notice.
[28]

[
18
]

Shortly after leaving the ICU, Mr. Douek also
had a telephone conversation with a lawyer he had known for approximately 10
years, Mtre Sydney Sweibel.
[29]
They spoke about Mr. Douek’s testamentary intentions as well as his
desire — which he had often expressed in the past — to avoid family conflicts.

[
19
]

As of mid-September 2012, Mr. Douek’s mental
status improved steadily.
[30]
The medical record also shows that he continued to be involved in
his company’s business during his hospitalization.
[31]

Moreover, Ms. Phillips was at his side on a daily basis and, on more than one
occasion, Mr. Douek told the medical team how fond he was of her.
[32]
He also expressed, later in September, the desire to leave the
hospital and go back home with her.
[33]

[
20
]

On Saturday, September 29, 2012, while he was
still hospitalized, Mr. Douek signed seven legal documents. All were prepared
by Mtre Derhy further to instructions he received from Mtre Sweibel as well as
from Mr. Douek’s daughters:

a)

Three of those documents relate to the transfer of Mr. Douek’s
hypothecary claim against his company — estimated then to be worth more than
two million dollars — to his two daughters. The documents consisted in a
one-page summary of the transaction,
[34]
a
four-page notarial act entitled “
Donation d’une créance hypothécaire
”
[35]
and a one-page notarial act whereby Mr. Douek released the
hypothec related to that claim.
[36]

b)

Mr. Douek also signed a five-page protection mandate
[37]
and a three-page power of attorney.
[38]

Both documents are notarial acts naming Mr. Douek’s daughters as his
representatives; they contain provisions that are commonly found in such
documents.

c)

Lastly, Mr. Douek signed two versions of his last will. One is a
three page, stripped-down version of the will which essentially mirrors the
provisions of the September 2 will while reiterating Mr. Douek’s intention to
transfer his hypothecary claim against his company to his two daughters.
[39]
The second version, identified as the “Testament principal”, is a
more comprehensive notarial will comprised of 25 pages.
[40]
It differs from the first version notably in that it contains
detailed provisions regarding the administration of Mr. Douek’s
succession. Ms. Phillips is mentioned in neither of these documents.

[
21
]

Mr. Douek passed away less than one month later,
on October 21, 2012.

II.
Substantive issues in dispute

A.

The defendants’ claims

[
22
]

While it is admittedly unusual to begin by
addressing claims made by a defending party, it is useful to do so here because
the analysis leads to findings that constitute contextual elements that are
relevant to Ms. Phillips’ claim of undue influence. The key point being
highlighted here is that the claims asserted by the defendants find so little
support in the record that one cannot help but infer from their actions an
inclination to resort to questionable means in order to resist claims made by
Ms. Phillips against their father’s succession.
[41]

1.   The claim of undue influence directed at Mr. Douek’s April 2012 will

[
23
]

In the written defence they filed in September
2014, the defendants allege that Mr. Douek’s April 2012 will was the
product of undue influence from Ms. Phillips. They assert that claim in the
alternative, should the Court come to the conclusion that the September 2012
wills were invalid. More specifically, the defendants — none of whom, it should
be noted, have first-hand knowledge of the circumstances surrounding the making
of the April 2012 will — ask the Court to draw an inference of undue influence
from the following facts:
[42]

•

since 2000, Mr. Douek had consistently expressed
the intention to only bequeath to Ms. Phillips, upon his death, his interest in
the Côte-Saint-Luc property — an intention he implicitly reiterated when he
made changes to his will in January 2012;

•

Ms. Phillips and Mr. Douek spent several weeks
together in Florida in the winter of 2012, thereby providing her with an
opportunity to pressure him;

•

in the April 2012 will, Mr. Douek appointed as
liquidators his daughters as well as an independent third party, while
providing that all decisions had to be made by a majority that had to include
that third party;

•

the April 2012 will includes a penalty clause
intended to discourage Mr. Douek’s daughters from challenging gifts he made to
Ms. Phillips;

•

the April 2012 will was made shortly after his
release from a hospital stay during which he was diagnosed with acute myeloid
leukemia;

•

the April 2012 is written in English, “Albert
Douek’s third language[,] and is of such complexity that a person with his
level of fluency would certainly have difficulty understanding”;
[43]

•

Mr. Douek’s daughters did nothing during the
winter of 2012 that could have led him to distrust them or make significant
changes to his earlier will.

[
24
]

By and of themselves, these facts fall well
short of supporting an inference that, in all likelihood, Mr. Douek made a new
will in April 2012 as a result of inappropriate pressure exerted on him by Ms.
Phillips.
[44]
Moreover, nothing in the compelling testimonies of
Mtre Sweibel, Mtre Malus and Mr. Schouela regarding the circumstances
surrounding the making of that will suggests that it was anything but the
expression of Mr. Douek’s true intentions.

[
25
]

It is worth adding that the defendants did not
insist on their claim of undue influence during the trial. When asked at the
beginning of the trial if their clients intended to maintain it, their lawyer
responded that he was not sure whether they would do so. Also — and tellingly—,
he did not press that claim during oral arguments.

2.   The claim that Ms. Phillips coerced Mr. Douek into transferring to
her his interest in the Côte-Saint-Luc property

[
26
]

In their statement of defence, the defendants
allege that Ms. Phillips harassed Mr. Douek into transferring to her his
interest in the Côte-Saint-Luc property and that, “[u]nable to resist [her]
incessant demands, [he] ultimately capitulated” and signed a deed of transfer
“which was prepared at [her] request and under the most questionable of
circumstances.”
[45]
The defendants further submit that this transaction amounted to a
gift that could be revoked,
inter alia
, on grounds of undue influence.

[
27
]

The assertion that Mr. Douek’s consent to the
transfer of his interest in the Côte-Saint-Luc property was vitiated by Ms.
Phillips’ harassing behaviour finds no support whatsoever in the evidence that
was adduced. Nothing in the compelling testimonies of Mtre Sweibel,
Mtre Malus and Mr. Schouela regarding the circumstances surrounding the
making of that transaction suggests that it was anything but the expression of
Mr. Douek’s true intentions.

[
28
]

It should also be noted that Ms. Rosen Douek was
unable to provide compelling answers to questions about this assertion when she
was examined out-of-court in October 2013. Her first answer was that Ms.
Phillips’ lawyers should simply ask their client about the circumstances
surrounding that transaction.
[46]
She then stated that she did not know how
Ms. Phillips had coerced Mr. Douek into agreeing to that transaction.
[47]
Shortly thereafter, she stated — without providing any specifics —
that Mr. Douek had told her that he had been coerced by Ms. Phillips into
giving her his half of the Côte-Saint-Luc property.
[48]

[
29
]

The defendants’ claim regarding the transfer of
that property is also one on which they did not insist during the trial. Their
lawyer even stated at one point that, out of what he claimed to be a desire on
their part to be gracious and fair to Ms. Phillips, they had decided to
withdraw that claim. However, he backtracked moments later and explained that
the claim ought to be considered withdrawn only in the event that the Court
ruled in his clients’ favour on the validity of the September 2012 wills. As
was the case with the defendants’ claim of undue influence directed at the
April 2012 will, this aspect of their case was not pressed during oral
arguments.

3.   The claim that Ms. Phillips misappropriated or attempted to
misappropriate hundreds of thousands of dollars

[
30
]

The defendants made very serious allegations to
the effect that, over a period of approximately ten months in 2011 and 2012, Ms.
Phillips misappropriated or attempted to misappropriate from Mr. Douek sums
totalling close to $430,000. At the heart of this contention is a series of
cheques, bearing dates ranging from October 20, 2011 to August 26, 2012, that
were purportedly made by Mr. Douek to Ms. Phillips.
[49]
The
defendants also claim that, on six occasions between February 2012 and August
2012, she unlawfully used one of Mr. Douek’s bank accounts to make payments to
her credit card issuer.
[50]
This aspect of their case forms the basis of their claim for the
reimbursement of more than $154,000 by Ms. Phillips. It is also central to
arguments of unworthiness (article 621
C.C.Q.
) and ingratitude (article
1836, 2
nd
para.
C.C.Q.
) that they have raised in relation to
various aspects of this case.

[
31
]

Up until the trial held in October 2019, the
defendants’ position regarding the cheques in dispute was that they had been
written and signed by Ms. Phillips herself. In support of their
contention, the defendants filed in June 2015 an expert report, authored by Ms.
Johanne E. Bergeron, tending to demonstrate that 23 cheques purportedly made by
Mr. Douek to Ms. Phillips between October 2011 and August 2012 bore
signatures that had been forged. In response, Ms. Phillips filed, in December
2015, a report, authored by Mr. Jean C. Dumont, tending to demonstrate that the
signatures found on those cheques had not been forged.

[
32
]

On the second day of the trial, while Mr. Dumont
was testifying in chief, the defendants announced that they were abandoning the
contention that the signatures found on the impugned cheques had been forged.
This significant shift, which one cannot help but view as an admission by the
defendants that their initial position was devoid of any merit, came with no
prior notice. Moreover, the defendants were unable to provide a compelling
answer when asked why they had waited until the very last minute to concede
that the signatures were indeed Mr. Douek’s. Their about-face, which is
clearly antithetical to the guiding principles underpinning our civil justice
system, provides further evidence of Mr. Douek’s daughters’ inclination to
resort to questionable means in order to resist claims made by Ms. Phillips against
their father’s succession.

[
33
]

Although the defendants now accept that the
cheques were signed by Mr. Douek, they have not abandoned their claim that Ms.
Phillips misappropriated or attempted to misappropriate sums totalling close to
$430,000 from Mr. Douek. However, their revised theory of the case is that Ms.
Phillips used pre-signed cheques that she filled out to herself without Mr. Douek’s
authorization.

[
34
]

The defendants have offered no direct evidence
in support of that theory. However, they argue that there is enough
circumstantial evidence in the record to support a finding that Mr. Douek never
authorized Ms. Phillips to write any of the cheques at issue. In particular,
they point to a number of allegedly unusual facts regarding the cheques — for
example the out-of-sequence numbering and the fact that some of them bear the
same date — as well as what they consider to be Ms. Phillips’ inability to
answer precisely, coherently and convincingly a number of questions about the
circumstances in which some of those cheques were made. On that last point,
they consider particularly suspicious the fact that Ms. Phillips was unable to
explain how two of the cheques came to be deposited in Montreal on dates when,
according to her earlier testimony, she was still in Florida with Mr. Douek.
[51]

[
35
]

The circumstantial evidence relied upon by the
defendants falls well short of giving rise to serious, precise and concordant
presumptions (article 2849
C.C.Q.
) supporting a finding that Ms. Phillips
engaged in a ten-month long criminal effort aimed at defrauding Mr. Douek.

[
36
]

While the defendants are right that Ms. Phillips
was unable to give precise and compelling answers to several questions that
were put to her in relation to the impugned cheques, they overlook the
likelihood that she was merely having trouble remembering specific facts that
had occurred more than seven years beforehand.

[
37
]

Furthermore — and most importantly —, it seems
highly implausible that Mr. Douek, an intelligent and sophisticated
businessman who was still professionally active throughout most of 2012, would
not have realized at some point that Ms. Phillips had misappropriated or
attempted to misappropriate hundreds of thousands of dollars from him.
Moreover, Ms. Phillips’ assertion that the impugned cheques represented gifts
from Mr. Douek is consistent with a broader pattern of end-of-life
generosity towards her — a pattern that is clearly evidenced by the facts that
he gave her $300,000 in 2011,
[52]
transferred to her half of the Côte-Saint-Luc property in
April 2012
[53]

and bought her a car worth nearly $100,000 shortly thereafter.
[54]
Mr. Douek’s
extensive generosity towards Ms. Phillips works against the defendants’
thesis in another way, as it makes it far less likely that she would have
deemed worthwhile to pursue a scheme aimed at obtaining further funds through
fraudulent means.

[
38
]

It should be added that the defendants have not
offered more compelling evidence tending to show that credit payments made by
Ms. Phillips between February 2012 and August 2012, using one of Mr. Douek’s
bank accounts, had not been properly authorized by him. This aspect of the
defendants’ claim must therefore be dismissed as well.

B.

Ms. Phillips’ claim of undue influence

[
39
]

The gist of Ms. Phillips’ claim of undue
influence is this: at some point in late August or early September 2012,
someone — in all likelihood Mr. Douek’s daughters — deceived Mr. Douek
into believing that Ms. Phillips was having an affair with a tennis pro, and
that belief explains why he made new wills containing no mention of a legacy of
$700,000 to Ms. Phillips.

[
40
]

During oral arguments, the defendants conceded
that the note Mr. Douek wrote to Mtre Derhy when they first met on
September 2, 2012
[55]

shows
that he had then formed the belief that Ms. Phillips was having an affair
with
a tennis pro. The defendants also conceded that it
was possible that Mr. Douek’s belief had led him to make new wills in which
Ms. Phillips was left out. However, they submit that Ms. Phillips has not
met her burden to prove that Mr. Douek had formed that belief as a result of
deceitful behaviour by the defendants. They further submit that Ms. Phillips
has failed to show that Mr. Douek’s belief was not only a possible reason,
but rather the probable reason why she was left out of the September 2012
wills.

1.   The applicable legal framework

[
41
]

There are two elements to a cause of action for
undue influence. The plaintiff must first prove “improper schemes, disgraceful
devices, lies, slander, deceit and trickery, or deliberate misrepresentations.”
[56]
The plaintiff must also prove that such machinations caused the
testator to make the impugned will.
[57]

[
42
]

Ms. Phillips has little to offer in the way of
direct evidence of undue influence, which means that her case is essentially
circumstantial. That is neither surprising nor fatal to her claim.

[
43
]

It is not surprising, because, as the Supreme
Court emphasized in 1979, “[p]roof of undue influence or suggestion sufficient
to vitiate the consent of a testator is not an easy undertaking, for it is rare
that the perpetrator of the manoeuvres employed, who stands to benefit from the
gift, operates directly and openly; if he is smart, he prefers to use oblique
and covert methods, which will enable him to achieve his objectives with greater
certainty and discretion.”
[58]

[
44
]

The fact that Ms. Phillips’ case is essentially
circumstantial is not fatal to her claim, because it is well established that
undue influence can be proved by presumptions of facts that meet the “serious,
precise and concordant” standard set out in article 2849
C.C.Q.
[59]
However, courts tend to carefully scrutinize circumstantial
evidence offered by the plaintiff, and they do not come to a finding of undue
influence lightly. This point is well illustrated by Court of Appeal decisions
standing for the proposition that proof of troubling facts and circumstances
surrounding the making of the impugned will, even when combined with incoherent
and misleading testimony by the defendant, will not necessarily suffice to
support a finding of undue influence.
[60]

[
45
]

That said, the need to rigorously scrutinize the
evidence does not entail a departure from the applicable standard of proof,
which remains proof on a balance of probabilities.
[61]

While judges “should not be unmindful, where appropriate, of inherent
probabilities or improbabilities or the seriousness of the allegations or
consequences,”
[62]
at the end of the day the question remains “whether it is more
likely than not”
[63]
that the impugned will was made as a result of “improper schemes,
disgraceful devices, lies, slander, deceit and trickery, or deliberate
misrepresentations.”
[64]
This conclusion also finds support in the analysis of proof by
presumptions of fact offered by Justice Louis Lebel, then of the Court of
Appeal, in
Lacasse c. Octave Labrecque ltée
:
[65]

Pour une preuve par présomption,
on
n’exige pas de dégager une certitude scientifique
.  On doit rechercher la
conclusion la plus rationnelle, à partir des éléments de fait connus.  Le
continuum entre l’improbable, l’hypothétique, le possible, le probable et le
certain ne se dégage pas toujours aisément.  L’opération d’induction conduisant
à la reconnaissance d’une présomption de fait,
suivant la norme civile des
probabilités
, peut
laisser une marge à un doute
.  Elle ne permet
pas, habituellement, d’atteindre à la certitude absolue ou scientifique — si
tant est que ces deux notions se confondent —
ni même à celle que requiert,
le plus souvent, le droit pénal, la preuve hors d’un doute raisonnable
.
Elle implique l’acceptation d’une solution comme
la plus plausible
,
comme
la plus raisonnable, à partir des faits trouvés
et après
constatation
qu’aucun autre facteur connu ne semble expliquer l’état de fait
observé de manière aussi rationnelle
(voir
Ferme Denijoy Inc. c. Société
coopérative agricole de St-Tite
, C.A. Québec, 26 mai
1994,
J.E. 94-912
, pp.
14-15
:

« L’appelante n’avait pas à offrir
une preuve ‘hors de tout doute’, comme le dit le docteur Panisset dans son
rapport d’expertise.  En matières civiles le critère est
celui de la
probabilité raisonnable
.  Pour prouver un lien de causalité entre la maladie
de son troupeau et le PRO-60, l’appelante
n’avait pas le fardeau de faire la
démonstration mathématiquement certaine que toutes les autres sources possibles
de contamination devaient être exclues
. »

[Emphasis added]

2.   Was Mr. Douek deceived into falsely believing that Ms. Phillips
was having an affair with a tennis pro?

[
46
]

The first issue to consider is what led Mr.
Douek to believe that Ms. Phillips was having an affair with a tennis pro.
Ms. Phillips submits that he developed that belief as a result of his daughters’
deceitful actions.

[
47
]

The defendants do not challenge Ms. Phillips’
adamant assertion that she was not having an affair at the time, but they deny
having had anything to do with Mr. Douek developing a belief to the contrary. They
also deny having been aware, in September 2012, that Mr. Douek had formed
that belief. They offer no alternative explanation as to how Mr. Douek became
convinced that Ms. Phillips was being unfaithful.

[
48
]

In my opinion, the analysis of the evidence
leads to the conclusion that it is more likely than not that Mr. Douek
developed that belief as a result of deceitful actions primarily carried out by
Ms. Rosen Douek.

[
49
]

To begin, it is worth making two observations
about the context in which the events of September 2012 took place.

[
50
]

The first is that, as is explained in the
previous section of this judgment, Mr. Douek’s daughters have shown a
willingness to go to great lengths in order to resist Ms. Phillips’ claims
against their father’s succession. Moreover, the penalty clause inserted in the
April 2012 will indicates that Mr. Douek considered his daughters capable of
taking unwarranted actions designed to prevent Ms. Phillips from benefiting
from assets or wealth he had transferred or intended to transfer to her. The
conclusion that can be drawn here is that, at the very least, it is not
inconceivable that Mr. Douek’s daughters deceived him into falsely believing
that Ms. Phillips was having an affair with a tennis pro. This is not one
of those cases where a person’s character — reflected in their past
behaviour — made it highly implausible that they had engaged in deceitful and
dishonest behaviour.

[
51
]

The second contextual element concerns Mr. Douek’s
situation in September 2012. It is clear from the testimonial evidence that was
adduced, notably from Mr. Edouard Schouela and Mtre Sydney Sweibel, that
Mr. Douek was not only a successful and wealthy entrepreneur, but also an
intelligent, independent and strong-willed man who — in all likelihood — was
not easily deceived. That said, it is just as clear that he was not in the best
form in September 2012. As indicated earlier, he was not only suffering from
acute myeloid leukemia, but he was also dealing with head injuries and
respiratory complications as a result of the fall he had sustained at the end
of August of that year. Therefore, in all likelihood, Mr. Douek was not as
impervious to undue influence as he probably had been beforehand.
[66]

[
52
]

A key element supporting Ms. Phillips’ claim of
undue influence is Ms. Santullo’s testimony. As mentioned earlier, Ms.
Santullo testified that she had overheard Ms. Rosen Douek telling other family
members that they had to convince her father to cut Ms. Phillips out of
his will, and that they ought to do so by telling him that Ms. Phillips had
been unfaithful. Ms. Santullo, who testified clearly and precisely about
the circumstances of that conversation and the manner in which she later made
the connection to Ms. Phillips, happens to be one of the few witnesses in
this case who are entirely independent from the parties. Furthermore, her
testimony is consistent with a sworn statement
[67]
she
signed years before she and Ms. Phillips even became aware of the existence
of Mr. Douek’s note about an affair involving a tennis pro
[68]
. There are no compelling reasons to discard her testimony as not
credible or unreliable.

[
53
]

Another element that supports Ms. Phillips’
thesis of undue influence is Mr. Schouela’s testimony. A close friend of and
longstanding advisor to Mr. Douek, Mr. Schouela visited him on several
occasions in September 2012. He testified convincingly to having then heard
from members of the Douek family rumours to the effect that Mr. Douek had
fallen early in the morning of August 30, 2012 as a result of having been
pushed by Ms. Phillips and a tennis player. Mr. Schouela’s testimony
is significant, because it tends to demonstrate that a rumour concerning Ms.
Phillips’ involvement with a tennis player was circulating among Mr. Douek’s
entourage at the time of his hospitalization. One would expect that, if such a rumour
reached Mr. Schouela at that time, it also would have reached Mr. Douek’s
daughters — especially Ms. Rosen Douek, given how close she remained to her
father throughout his hospitalization. Yet — and as their lawyer emphasized
during oral arguments —, the defendants have always denied having then been
aware of rumours of Ms. Phillips’ infidelity or involvement with a tennis pro.
Mr. Schouela’s testimony raises serious doubts about the credibility of the
defendants’ denials.

[
54
]

These concerns are compounded by answers given
by Ms. Rosen Douek when she was examined out-of-court in October 2013, merely
one year after the events. Ms. Phillips is right that many of her answers
were problematic to the point of conveying the impression that she was not
willing to tell the truth and that she had something to hide. Illustrative
examples include the following:

a)

she claimed to be in possession of a writing by Mr. Douek accusing
Ms. Phillips of having pushed him early in the morning of August 30, 2012,
[69]
but she never produced such a writing, which is not surprising
given how unlikely it is that Mr. Douek ever made such an accusation,
whether in writing or otherwise;

b)

she categorically denied being aware of other legal documents having
been signed on September 2, 2012,
[70]
yet
it is clear that she not only provided Mtre Derhy with the quit claim deed
executed on that day, she also signed it as a witness;
[71]

c)

she denied having signed any document on September 29, 2012, when
Mtre Derhy visited Mr. Douek for the second time,
[72]
yet
it is clear that she then signed the “
Donation d’une créance
hypothécaire
”
[73]

that Mtre Derhy had previously prepared;

d)

she stated that when Ms. Edwards — the representative of Mr. Douek’s
bank — called him on September 6, 2012 to enquire about the $275,000 cheque, Mr. Douek
was very upset and denied having ever made it,
[74]
yet
Ms. Edwards testified convincingly that the conversation she had had with Mr.
Douek on that day had been normal and that he had merely told her that he had
no recollection of having written the cheque;

e)

her assertion that she was “a hundred percent” certain that Mr.
Douek never fully read the April 2012 will
[75]

lacks credibility, not only because she wasn’t present when that will was
signed, but also because that assertion is both highly implausible and
impossible to reconcile with Mtre Sweibel and Mtre Malus’ compelling
testimonies about the manner in which that will was prepared and executed;
[76]

f)

similarly, her categorical assertion that Mr. Douek wrote the wills
that he signed on September 29, 2012
[77]
is
not only highly implausible — how could he have done so? —, it is also
contradicted by Mtre Derhy’s testimony about the manner in which those wills
were prepared;

g)

moments after having stated that, while in the hospital in September
2012, her father had told Ms. Phillips that he intended to change his will, she
contradicted herself by stating that Mr. Douek had sought to make sure that Ms.
Phillips would not be suspicious of his intention to make a new will
[78]
.

[
55
]

Other elements of the record indicate that, in
September 2012, Mr. Douek’s daughters intervened in his affairs in ways that tend
to support, although to varying degrees, Ms. Phillips’ thesis. One example is
Mtre Derhy’s testimony to the effect that, when he first met with Mr.
Douek on September 2, 2012, Ms. Rosen Douek — who was present for most of the
meeting — told her father to tell Mtre Derhy that he wished to cut
Ms. Phillips out of his will. Another example is that Ms. Rosen Douek,
who was with her father when he spoke with Ms. Edwards on September 6,
2012, was the one who drafted the letter asking the bank to freeze his
accounts.
[79]
A third example is Ms. Madger Douek’s statement to the effect
that she urged her father to freeze another bank account in order to prevent
Ms. Phillips from making any use of it.
[80]
Yet
another example is an excerpt of Mr. Douek’s medical record showing that, on
September 5, 2012, Ms. Rosen Douek insisted on being the only family
member who needed to be present to an upcoming meeting with the medical team.
[81]

[
56
]

The significant involvement of Mr. Douek’s
daughters in their father’s affairs is also reflected in the circumstances
surrounding the preparation and execution of the seven legal documents he
signed on September 29, 2012. It is clear from Mtre Derhy’s testimony as well
as the exhibits that have been filed
[82]

that any instructions he received in relation to those documents came primarily
from Mr. Douek’s daughters, who were also in contact at that time with
Mtre Sweibel. Moreover, Mtre Derhy testified that he had not spoken to Mr.
Douek about the documents before meeting with him — for the second and last
time — on September 29, 2012, and there is no evidence tending to
demonstrate that Mr. Douek was involved in any way in their preparation.
The record also shows that Mtre Derhy reviewed the documents with both Ms.
Rosen Douek and Ms. Magder Douek, before presenting them to Mr. Douek during a
meeting that lasted no more than 45 to 60 minutes.
[83]

[
57
]

In sum, the record shows the following:

•

on September 2, 2012, Mr. Douek had formed the
belief that Ms. Phillips was having an affair with a tennis pro;

•

Ms. Phillips’ denial of unfaithfulness was not
challenged by the defendants and nothing in the record can support a finding
that Mr. Douek’s belief was actually true;

•

in early September 2012, while her father was
still in the ICU, Ms. Rosen Douek expressed the intention to tell her father
that Ms. Phillips was having an affair in order to convince him to change his
will;

•

the manner in which Mr. Douek’s daughters
responded to Ms. Phillips’ claims, along with Mr. Douek’s belief that they
were capable of taking unwarranted actions against Ms. Phillips, show that it
is very much plausible that they deceived him into falsely believing that she
was having an affair with a tennis pro;

•

Mr. Douek’s daughters remained close to their
father and were significantly involved in his affairs throughout the hospitalization
that preceded his death;

•

a rumour concerning Ms. Phillips’ involvement
with a tennis player was circulating among the Douek family at the time of Mr.
Douek’s hospitalization, and because it is unlikely that this rumour failed to
reach Mr. Douek’s daughters, their denial of having had any knowledge — at that
time — of an affair involving Ms. Phillips and a tennis player is not credible;

•

in several respects, the transcript of Ms. Rosen
Douek’s examination out-of-court conveys the impression that she had little
interest in telling the truth and had something to hide.

These facts support
an inference that Mr. Douek developed a belief that Ms. Phillips was having an
affair with a tennis pro as a result of deceitful actions primarily carried out
by Ms. Rosen Douek. Moreover, because these facts cannot support an equally
compelling alternative explanation — let alone a more compelling one —
regarding the source of Mr. Douek’s belief, I find that it is more likely
than not that Mr. Douek developed that belief as a result of his daughter’s
deceitful actions. Ms. Phillips has thus met her burden on that aspect of the
case.

3.   Did Mr. Douek make the September 2012
wills because he believed that Ms. Phillips was having an affair with a
tennis pro?

[
58
]

As mentioned earlier, the defendants conceded that
it is possible that Mr. Douek made new wills in September 2012 because he
had then formed the belief that Ms. Phillips was having an affair with a
tennis pro. However, they contend that Ms. Phillips has failed to show that
Mr. Douek’s belief was not only a possible reason, but actually the
probable reason she was left out of the September 2012 wills.

[
59
]

The starting point of the analysis on the issue
of causation is Mr. Douek’s handwritten note to Mtre Derhy about the tennis pro.
[84]
That note tends to support Ms. Phillips’
position, as logic and common sense suggest quite strongly that Mr. Douek
mentioned the tennis pro to Mtre Derhy because he wished to explain his
decision to leave Ms. Phillips out of his new will. If he was not bothered by
the thought of Ms. Phillips being unfaithful, and if he had other reasons to
exclude her from his last will — one possibility being a tax liability issue on
which Mtre Sweibel testified and which could have had a significant impact on
the size of his succession —, why would he have written that note to
Mtre Derhy?

[
60
]

This conclusion is reinforced by Mtre Derhy’s
own testimony. He was the only other person in the room when Mr. Douek wrote
the note, and he stated under oath that it was clear to him — given the context
in which the note had been written — that Mr. Douek was implicitly
conveying the message that Ms. Phillips’ purported unfaithfulness was the
reason why she was not mentioned in his new will. The defendants are hardly in
a position to question the probative value of Mtre Derhy’s testimony, as they
have insisted throughout the proceeding that he was a compelling witness whose
competence and credibility could not seriously be disputed.

[
61
]

The defendants argue that a number of
circumstantial facts tend to rebut any inference of causation that could be
drawn from Mr. Douek’s note and Mtre Derhy’s testimony. In particular, they
insist on the fact that Ms. Phillips was at Mr. Douek’s bedside throughout his
hospitalization and that the medical record shows that he occasionally
expressed his fondness for her as well as his wish to return home in her
company.
[85]
According to the defendants, Mr. Douek would not have spoken kindly
of Ms. Phillips, nor would he have let her stay at his bedside, if his belief
in her unfaithfulness had troubled him to the point where he would have deemed
necessary to change his will. The defendants add that Mr. Douek had
himself been unfaithful to Ms. Goliger Douek after meeting Ms. Phillips in the
1980s, which suggests that he would not have been particularly concerned upon
learning of her purported unfaithfulness.

[
62
]

The defendants also point to the fact that Mr.
Douek never mentioned to either Mr. Schouela or Mtre Sweibel that he had
changed his will because he had come to believe that Ms. Phillips had been
unfaithful. Similarly, the defendants consider relevant the fact that
Mr. Douek never mentioned Ms. Phillips’ purported unfaithfulness when he
spoke to Ms. Edwards on September 6, 2012 and asked her to freeze his bank
account.

[
63
]

In my opinion, none of these circumstantial
facts rebut the inference of causation that flows from Mr. Douek’s note and
Mtre Derhy’s testimony. The reason lies in the fact that they can support an
alternative narrative that is both equally compelling and consistent with the
theory of causation put forward by Ms. Phillips. Indeed, while Mr. Douek
was in all likelihood unhappy to learn about Ms. Phillips’ purported
unfaithfulness — to the point where he felt he had to exclude her from his will
—, it is very much plausible that he nevertheless preferred not to confront her
and to make sure she would be by his bedside during his hospitalization. He
could have had a number of reasons, from the highly emotional to the very
practical, for doing so. This is all the more plausible since — as explained by
Mtre Sweibel — Mr. Douek had always been careful, over the years, to avoid
creating or exacerbating family conflicts.

[
64
]

Another noteworthy contextual element is the
fact that Mr. Douek never sought to completely exclude Ms. Goliger Douek from
his life even though she had herself been unfaithful during their marriage.
[86]
He even intended to leave her a significant part of his succession
in the wills he made in 2000 and April 2012.
[87]

This increases the likelihood that, upon learning about Ms. Phillips’ purported
unfaithfulness, Mr. Douek had a somewhat moderate reaction — deciding to
exclude her from his will in order to leave more to Ms. Goliger Douek and
daughters, but not openly confronting her to avoid having to deal with conflict
during his dying days.

[
65
]

Furthermore, I am not convinced that much can be
inferred from the fact that Mr. Douek made no mention of Ms. Phillips’
purported unfaithfulness to either Mtre Sweibel or Ms. Edwards. It is not
hard to imagine reasons why Mr. Douek may have preferred not to share with either
of them his belief that Ms. Phillips had been seeing someone else. This surely
explains why the defendants’ lawyer conceded during oral arguments that it was
possible that Mr. Douek had chosen not to be fully transparent when, shortly
after leaving the ICU, he spoke with Mtre Sweibel about his decision to make a
new will.

[
66
]

The defendants point to another circumstantial
fact which, in their opinion, cannot be reconciled with the inference that Ms.
Phillips asks the Court to draw from Mr. Douek’s note and Mtre Derhy’s
testimony. That fact is Mr. Douek’s reaction to Ms. Phillips’ queries about the
$275,000 cheque she deposited in her bank account on August 31, 2012.
[88]
Ms. Phillips testified that, after telling him that the funds
had disappeared from her account, Mr. Douek had asked her to bring him another
cheque.
[89]
The defendants argue that Mr. Douek would never have reacted
in that manner if he had been troubled by Ms. Phillips’ purported
unfaithfulness to the point where he had felt necessary to change his will.

[
67
]

However, Mr. Douek reaction’s is not as
incompatible with Ms. Phillips’ theory of the case on causation as the
defendants believe it to be. The notes Mr. Douek wrote to Mtre Derhy on
September 2, 2012 show that he had no issue with Ms. Phillips keeping what he
had already given her: “
[c]e que j’ai donné elle Roslyn PHILLIPS peut
le garder.
”
[90]

Mr. Douek wrote that note after the $275,000 cheque was made but before
speaking to Ms. Edwards, which means that, at that time, that $275,000
gift formed part of what he had already given Ms. Phillips. For that reason,
the fact that he subsequently asked Ms. Phillips to bring him another
cheque can be viewed as consistent with his wish that she keep whatever she had
already received: the new cheque would not have been a new or additional gift,
but rather a means for Ms. Phillips to properly take possession of a gift that he
had made prior to September 2, 2012.

[
68
]

For these reasons, I find that Ms. Phillips has established
on a balance of probabilities that Mr. Douek made the September 2, 2012 will as
a result of deceitful actions primarily carried out by Ms. Rosen Douek. This
conclusion is also applicable to the will signed by Mr. Douek on September 29,
2012. As Mtre Derhy explained during the trial, that last will was essentially
aimed at confirming Mr. Douek’s September 2, 2012 will while adding detailed
provisions regarding the administration of his succession. Nothing in the
record suggests that the provisions of the September 29, 2012 will concerning
the distribution of Mr. Douek’s property were based on different considerations
than those underlying the corresponding provisions of the September 2, 2012
will.

[
69
]

The September 2012 wills must therefore be annulled
on grounds of undue influence.

C.

Ms. Phillips’ claim for the sum of
$275,000

[
70
]

Ms. Phillips is claiming the sum of $275,000 from
Mr. Douek’s succession, which corresponds to the amount indicated on the cheque
she deposited on August 31, 2012. As mentioned earlier, that sum was debited
from Mr. Douek’s account and credited to Ms. Phillips’ account five days
later. Shortly thereafter, after a verification triggered by the transaction’s
amount, the funds were transferred back to Mr. Douek’s account.

[
71
]

Ms. Phillips’ position is that the sum of
$275,000 was validly gifted to her within the meaning of article 1824
C.C.Q.
,
which reads as follows:

1824
.

The gift of movable or immovable property is made,
on pain of absolute nullity, by notarial act
en minute
, and shall be
published.

These rules do not apply where,
in
the case of the gift of movable property
, the consent of the parties
is
accompanied by delivery and immediate possession of the property
.

1824.
La donation d’un bien meuble ou immeuble
s’effectue, à peine de nullité absolue, par acte notarié en minute; elle doit
être publiée.

Il est fait exception à
ces règles lorsque,
s’agissant de la donation d’un bien meuble
, le
consentement des parties
s’accompagne de la délivrance et de la possession
immédiate du bien
.

[Emphasis added]

Relying on judgments from the Court of
Appeal, Ms. Phillips argues that a pecuniary gift may be validly made by a
banking operation of the kind that occurred in the present case.
[91]

[
72
]

The defendants’ main argument in response to Ms. Phillips’ claim,
which is that Mr. Douek never authorized Ms. Phillips to write a cheque to
herself in the amount of $275,000, must fail for reasons that were set out
earlier.
[92]

[
73
]

The defendants contend in the alternative that the gift is null
as having been made
mortis causa
. That argument rests on article 1820, 1
st
para.

C.C.Q.
, which provides that a gift made during “the deemed mortal
illness/
la maladie réputée mortelle
” of the donor is null unless it is
shown that the donation would have been made notwithstanding the donor’s
impending death.
[93]

Whether a gift was indeed made during a deemed mortal illness is to be analyzed
both objectively and subjectively: the illness must have been so serious that
death was objectively imminent, and the donor must have been aware — when
the gift was made — that the seriousness of their condition was such that death
was likely to be imminent.
[94]

[
74
]

There is little doubt, objectively speaking, that Mr. Douek was
gravely ill at the end of August 2012, less than two months before he passed
away as a result of his leukemia.
[95]

As the expert retained by Ms. Phillips himself recognized, Mr. Douek was
— throughout his hospitalization — “terminally ill with a blood cancer and
a number of related medical ailments.”
[96]
For his part, the
expert retained by the defendants noted in his report that, when he was
diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia in the winter of 2012,
Mr. Douek was given two to six months to live.
[97]

[
75
]

Moreover, Mr. Douek was in all likelihood well aware of the
seriousness of his condition at the end of August 2012. By all accounts, he was
a very intelligent man, and he must have clearly understood the gravity of a
diagnosis of acute myeloid leukemia for a man of his age. It
is also noteworthy that Ms. Phillips admitted during her examination on
discovery that, when he had told her that he wished her to have an additional
sum of $275,000, Mr. Douek was aware of his illness and had acted as he had
with a view to protecting her.
[98]

Those facts, combined with the significance of the amount involved, strongly
suggest not only that Mr. Douek was then fully aware that he was gravely ill,
but also that he made that gift to Ms. Phillips because he knew that he did not
have very long to live.

[
76
]

As nothing in the record can support a finding that Mr. Douek
would have made that gift to Ms. Phillips notwithstanding his impending death,
the defendants’
mortis causa
argument is well founded. Therefore, even
assuming that the sum of $275,000 was gifted to Ms. Phillips in a manner that
complies with the provisions of article 1824
C.C.Q.
, her claim sum must
fail.

D.

Conclusion

[
77
]

Ms. Phillips has successfully challenged the validity of the
notarial wills made by Mr. Douek in September 2012, and the defendants have
failed to establish that the April 2012 will was invalid on grounds of
undue influence. The defendants have also failed to establish that Ms. Phillips
had misappropriated or attempted to misappropriate substantial sums of money
from Mr. Douek, which entails — among other things — that their argument of
unworthiness directed at the April 2012 will must dismissed as well.

[
78
]

It does not automatically ensue that Ms. Phillips is owed
$700,000 by Mr. Douek’s succession. The defendants raised a last-minute
argument to the effect that her $700,000 claim should fail
even if the September 2012 notarial wills were declared invalid. Their argument
is based on the fact that Ms. Phillips never expressly challenged the validity
of a note, written on September 2, 2012, in which Mr. Douek expressed to
Mtre Derhy his intention to revoke his previous wills and leave one half
of his property to Ms. Goliger Douek and the other half to his two daughters
[99]
. The defendants contend that this handwritten note, which bears Mr.
Douek’s signature, constitutes a valid holograph will that ought to be
recognized as his true last will in the event that the September 2 and 29
notarial wills were held to be invalid.

[
79
]

The defendants’ argument fails. Ms. Phillips’
lawyers were right to point out that the relevant conclusion of their client’s
originating application
[100]
is broad enough to cover that handwritten note. Had that not been
the case, I would not have hesitated to grant Ms. Phillips’
de bene
esse
application to amend that conclusion, as it would certainly have been
in the interest of justice to do so.

[
80
]

Ms. Phillips thus succeeds on her $700,000 claim
based on the April 2012 will, which is Mr. Douek’s true last will. However, her
$275,000 claim based on the August 31, 2012 cheque must be dismissed as that
cheque constitutes a gift that was made
mortis causa
.

[
81
]

Lastly, the defendants have failed to establish the invalidity of
the April 2012 transaction relating to the Côte-Saint-Luc property. Their
ingratitude argument must be dismissed because they have not shown that Ms. Phillips
had misappropriated or attempted to misappropriate substantial sums of money
from Mr. Douek. They have also failed to meet their burden of showing that
Mr. Douek had been coerced into agreeing to that transaction.

III.
Solicitor-client fees and legal costs

[
82
]

The defendants are asking that Ms. Phillips
be ordered to bear the entirety of their solicitor-client fees — which total no
less than $424,264 —, on the grounds that she acted abusively in the course of
the present proceeding (articles 51 et seq
C.C.P.
).

[
83
]

Given the outcome of this case, it certainly cannot
be said that Ms. Phillips’ originating application as a whole constitutes an
abuse of process justifying that she be ordered to pay the defendants’
solicitor-client fees in their entirety. And while the defendants are right to
point out that Ms. Phillips has engaged — mainly through her lawyers — in
reprehensible conduct on several occasions
[101]
,
the fact of the matter is that, on both sides
[102]
,
this case has been litigated with a deplorable disregard for several of the
guiding principles and fundamental values — including cooperation, good faith
and forbearance — that are key to the proper functioning of our civil
justice system. For that reason, and also because of the mixed outcome of this
case, each party will bear their legal costs and no order will be made
regarding solicitor-client fees.

For example, in February 2013, Ms. Phillips’ lawyers wrote to the

Another example is Ms. Phillips’ last-minute decision to abandon a claim in the
amount of $375,000 based on the penalty clause found in the April 2012
will. A further example is the fact that she had no valid reason to include Ms.
Goliger Douek as a defendant to her action, nor did she have any reason to
include Mss. Madger Douek and Rosen Douek personally as defendants to her
claims in the amounts of $700,000 and $275,000. Moreover, the defendants were
right to deplore Ms. Phillips’ lack of transparency regarding whether she would
insist on calling Ms. Magder Douek as a witness during the October 2019
trial.
